claims.text: Introducing a controlled dwell near the peak synthesis temperature will enhance atomic mixing and promote homogeneous single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles.
Moderately slower heating and cooling rates will enhance atomic mixing and single-phase formation relative to rapid heating and cooling.
The relevant materials are noble-metal nanoparticles made from single-source precursors containing more than five elements.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling tends to produce phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology in these materials.
A peak synthesis temperature around 1100 K is applicable to formation of multielement solid-solution nanoparticles.
At approximately 1100 K, transient atomic mobility can enable elemental mixing without excessive nanoparticle growth if the high-temperature exposure is limited.
Transient atomic diffusion and mixing during the dwell mediates uniform incorporation of the constituent metals into a single-phase lattice.
The dwell increases atomic mobility enough to overcome kinetic limitations imposed by rapid thermal cycles.
Improved diffusion during the dwell prevents compositionally segregated regions.
Improved diffusion during the dwell prevents crystallographic defects that lead to phase separation.
A limited dwell can permit structural evolution while avoiding nanoparticle growth or agglomeration.
The modified thermal profile will yield a higher fraction of uniformly mixed, single-phase nanoparticles than the rapid-cycle baseline.
The modified profile will reduce elemental segregation and phase separation relative to the baseline.
Rapid cycles with negligible dwell typically kinetically trap locally segregated phases and inconsistent particle morphologies.
Increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more probable when free-atom mobility is limited.
The intervention is expected to be significant specifically for noble-metal systems containing at least five elements near 1100 K under rapid processing.
At extremely high temperatures, excessive diffusion will cause agglomeration and make the intervention ineffective.
The optimal dwell duration and ramp rates vary with alloy composition and elemental interactions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in single-phase formation, segregation, and phase separation relative to an identical rapid-cycle control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The target is initially defined as containing more than five elements, but the boundary is broadened to at least five elements without explaining the inclusion of exactly five-element systems.
